# How to read this document

This is a record of where the enzyme- and temperature-constrained genome-scale model (etcGEM)
work stands, written for the three of us. It covers the **framework** — the shared core, the
seven organism models on it, and what has been learned by testing them. Empirical work appears
only where the framework consumes it: measured thermal performance curves as calibration or
validation targets, the measured meltome as a predictor benchmark, measured activation energies
as comparators. The Candida manuscript's own empirical results are not ours to assess and are
not assessed here.

**Every number in this document comes from a file.** `evidence.csv` in this directory carries one
row per claim: the value, the file, the commit that last wrote that file, and whether the claim
is CURRENT, HISTORICAL (true of an earlier model state) or PROVISIONAL-ON-P6. Claims are cited
by their row id, like [W1]. Nothing is quoted from memory or from another summary.

**Several of the sharpest findings came from correcting things this project itself got wrong.**
Those are in §[-@sec-own], with the same prominence as everything else. That section is not
throat-clearing: two of the seven changed a conclusion.

A caution that applies throughout. A large fraction of this week's results are **negative** —
things that do not work, do not generalise, or turn out to be arithmetic. Some negatives are
valuable because they close a question or invalidate a comparison; others are simply absent
effects. §[-@sec-pub] distinguishes them where it matters, and does not inflate either kind.

# Where things stood {#sec-start}

Two implementations of the same idea existed side by side [W1]. `src/etcgem` carried three
organisms — *E. coli*, *M. maripaludis*, *Synechocystis* — with a config model, providers, one
thermal layer and one enzyme-cost layer [W2]. Ilgaz's `gem/` carried four *Candida* species with
its own thermal function, its own path map and species handled by a dictionary. Parsa's six
gas-exchange configurations sat on a July snapshot of the core with new modules beside it.

Nothing was wrong with any of them individually. The problem was that the method existed in
three places, so a change in one could not be checked against the others, and the published
*Candida* result rested on numbers whose absolute scale nobody could reproduce from the shared
code.

# The merge, and what the gates prove {#sec-merge}

Both bodies of work are now on one core. Four *Candida* strains are `strains/` folders carrying
data and configuration and no code [W3]; Parsa's configurations are `configs/experiments/`
overlays and one CLI verb. Seven organism models share one thermal layer, one enzyme-cost layer
and one config model.

Three gates hold that together, and all three are re-run at every merge:

| gate | what it proves | result |
|---|---|---|
| K1 | the *Candida* port reproduces the standalone implementation | **79/79 PASS** [G1] |
| P1 | configurations A, B and C reproduce Parsa's committed gas-flux numbers | **60/60 PASS**, worst difference 8.3×10⁻⁴ [G2, G3] |
| P3 | configurations D, E and F reproduce the R² his reports print | **10 of 10, worst 0.009** [G4] |

The K1 gate reproduces the standalone *including a ~0.4 % error its own solver made* at two
points, which is why the repository now distinguishes **fidelity to the original** from
**numerical correctness** and keeps both configurations. His v3 posterior is identical to the one
committed here to every stored digit [G5], so the two codebases share a calibration and not just
a method.

**What a gate does not prove.** It checks the fields it compares. The P3 gate evaluates one
parameter point once, after a fresh build, on both sides — as a *port* check it stands. It says
nothing about whether the quantity being scored is well defined, which §[-@sec-sampling] returns
to.

# What the models turned out to be doing {#sec-shortcuts}

The most consequential class of finding this week was not about temperature at all. It is that
these reconstructions contain **uncosted shortcuts**: routes that carry flux without paying the
enzyme cost the whole method is built on. Four instances, three organisms, one of them in a
published reconstruction.

**E. coli: four O₂ sinks.** Four O₂-consuming side reactions carry ~zero enzyme cost and
short-circuit the electron transport chain, creating a futile cycle that was ~75 % of gross O₂
turnover at LB/40 °C. Closing them costs ~0.3 % growth and is now a provider default [S1]. This
was Parsa's audit, and it is the template for the rest.

**The three *Candidozyma*: a free proton circuit.** Their respiratory chain supplies **0.04–0.05 %**
of the protons ATP synthase consumes; *C. parapsilosis* supplies 112 % and *E. coli* 124 % [S2].
Eleven uncosted, **reversible** metabolite/H⁺ symporters close the circuit outside the chain. The
separating feature is reversibility, not uncostedness: *E. coli* has twelve uncosted proton
movers and none reversible [S3]. Constraining the direction repairs it at a cost of 36–38 % of
predicted growth [S4]; costing the transport does not. The defect is in the published *iRV973*,
verified read-only, and is shared by the three models derived from it.

**And a second defect in the same scaffold:** complex III moves its protons cytosol→matrix, the
opposite direction to a mitochondrion, so it *spends* the gradient rather than building it [S5].

**The audit had a blind spot, and it was structural.** `etcgem audit-sinks` watched chemical
carriers and terminal acceptors — classes A to D. **None watched the ion ATP synthase runs on**
[S6]. A free proton circuit passed an audit that reported 44–47 class-A hits in the same models.
Class E now covers it, and getting it right required three things that would each have
mis-diagnosed an organism: inferring the coupling ion per strain (*M. maripaludis* is
sodium-driven [S7]), counting chemistry as well as translocation (*Synechocystis* scores 19 % on
translocation and 100 % with the lumen's water splitting counted), and handling GECKO's
arm/isozyme split (a naive test finds no ATP synthase in *eciML1515* at all).

**What this means for the method, stated carefully.** An enzyme-constrained model's central claim
is that flux costs protein. A route that carries flux for free is not a modelling approximation;
it is a hole in that claim, and it is invisible to every check that looks at growth. Four have now
been found by looking, and the fourth was found only because a class of check did not exist. That
is a statement about how these reconstructions are built and audited, not about any one of them.

# What the predictors turned out to be doing {#sec-predictors}

Every species-specific input the *Candida* etcGEM has comes from sequence predictors. A1 tested
the load-bearing one against measurement.

**Seq2Tm resolves thermostability between organisms and not within a proteome.** Across the tree
of life, r = **+0.762** [A1]. Within one proteome, against 1947 measured *S. cerevisiae* melting
points, r = **−0.048** [A2]. Where it can be checked against a measured congeneric difference it
under-states it **17-fold** [A3].

**The bias is not uniform, and that matters more than its size.** The mean is +5.43 °C [A4], but
it rises **1.06 °C per °C of predicted Tm** — from +2.44 °C in the lowest predicted octile to
+12.78 °C in the highest [A5]. The cause is A1's own headline: measured Tm barely responds to the
prediction (slope −0.061 [A6]), so almost all of the predicted spread is error, and the error
grows with the prediction. A flat offset therefore corrects the *location* of the Tm distribution
and not its *shape*.

**What could not be obtained.** Per-protein measured *S. cerevisiae*/*S. uvarum* Tm; the authors
publish the summary only [A8]. So the strongest test — the correlation of measured against
predicted *differences* — cannot be computed, and the congeneric comparison is summary to
summary. Nothing was substituted for it.

# What sets a thermal curve in these models {#sec-curve}

Three separate constraints have each been shown to relocate the growth optimum, on the same
organism and model:

| constraint | effect on $T_\text{opt}$ | effect on $CT_\text{max}$ |
|---|---|---|
| the sector re-grounding (`a416fd1`) | 37 → 30 °C [T1] | +0.05 % |
| the translation cap, where it binds | $T_\text{opt}$ *is* where the cap starts to bind [T2] | unmoved |
| a total-carbon cap | 39.0 → 32.5 °C between $c_\text{max}$ 80 and 60 [T3] | ≤0.66 % [T4] |

The pattern is mechanical rather than coincidental. $CT_\text{max}$ is where the unfolding
envelope takes growth to zero, and a capacity constraint can only lower the curve — it cannot
move the temperature at which enzymes denature. $T_\text{opt}$ is wherever the *binding*
constraint's ceiling peaks or crosses the rising envelope-limited branch, so it moves whenever
**which** constraint binds changes, with no change to the envelope at all.

The standing rule that follows is now written down: **$T_\text{opt}$ is quoted with its binding
constraint named; $CT_\text{max}$ may be quoted plainly** [T5]. A variance decomposition that
reports "$T_\text{opt}$ is owned by protein stability" is a statement about one operating point,
measured with local perturbations that do not cross a regime boundary. It is not wrong; it is
conditional, and the condition is now stated in the E. coli report.

**Two structural limitations of the growth envelope, found separately.** The model's growth
activation energy is too steep against measurement in every *Candida* species, by **1.24–2.29×**,
and the error barely moves between configurations — it is structural, not a tuning failure [T7].
About **88 %** of it is the shared ΔCp prior [T8]; a value inside the literature range reconciles
the activation energy *and* improves the fit. But the same parameter **cannot** close the ceiling
over-prediction and pushes it slightly the wrong way [T9]: two failures, not one failure with one
cause.

And one artefact worth knowing about because it looks like biology: the *E. coli* glucose
proteome was measured at 25, 30 and 37 °C only, so above 37 °C the allocation is held constant
and the nominal curve is **bit-identical across eight grid points** at 0.524757 h⁻¹ [T6]. The
model is answering the same question eight times; the shoulder is the data table running out.

# The arithmetic behind the *Candida* figure {#sec-figure}

Figure 4's claim is a ratio: the Tm separation the model *requires* between relatives, over the
separation the predictors say is *available*. Both halves have moved, for different reasons, and
the sequence is the finding.

![**Figure 4's arithmetic, stage by stage.** **A)** the Tm separation the model requires between
relatives, at four model states, against the only measured congeneric benchmark there is
(1.6 °C over 827 ortholog pairs, dashed). **B)** the fold gap that constitutes the claim, with
A1's two corrections and the credible interval on the corrected value. Every value is read from a
committed table; producing script `reports/synthesis/fig_requirement_arithmetic.py`, sources named
in its docstring.](assets/figures/requirement_arithmetic.png){#fig-arith width=100%}

**The requirement fell by more than half when the model changed, and has been stable since.**
32.54 °C as published [F1]; 13.77 °C once it runs on this repository's thermal form (K2), and
13.64 °C on this repository's own recompute of that state; **13.57 °C** after the K5 proton-circuit
repair [F3]. It is also **convention-independent** — the two growth conventions differ by 0.00 °C
on the repaired model [F4] — because the counterfactual makes zero calls to the predicted strain's
measured curve. That retires a worry about a number already in circulation.

**The available separation rose 6-fold when the predictor was corrected**, from 0.411 °C to
2.56 °C [1.33, 5.56], and the fold gap with it: **~79× → 34× → 5.4× [2.5, 10.3]** [A7]. Still a
failure, and a materially different sentence.

**Two things about the remaining gap.** First, applying A1's measured bias — untuned, at exactly
the value A1 measured — closes the ceiling gaps by **a third to a half** in all four species, and
the rising limb does not move [F8]. Full closure would need **1.8–2.8× that bias, differing by
5 °C between species** [F9], which no uniform predictor bias can produce. Second, and this is the
harder constraint: the model's $CT_\text{max}$ spans **1.6 °C** across the four species while the
**observed** limits span **6 °C** [F10]. The variation in the gap is almost entirely
observational, so no uniform correction can differentially fix the gaps — only their average.

**And the interspecies requirement turns out to be arithmetic, not a model constraint** [F6].
Recomputing the required per-species offset under five model states, the model's own ceiling
spread varies **4.5-fold** while the required-offset spread moves by **±3 %**, pinned to the
observed 6.00 °C throughout. The interspecies difference is the observed thermal-limit difference
wearing a model's clothes, and must not be set beside a measured congeneric difference as though
the two were commensurable. What survives is the *per-species* statement — "this model's ceiling
is 9.8 °C too high for *C. auris*" is a real model statement — and that is what §[-@sec-pub] uses.

The other candidate explanation did not generalise either: the ~5.6 K common ceiling term that
looked like it might be shared is a **one-organism observation**, with residuals spanning
0.05–10.48 °C across the strains where they can be computed [F7].

# The membrane-area mechanism {#sec-membrane}

P1 collapsed Parsa's configurations E and F into one table-driven ETC membrane-area constraint in
the core — an area budget $\sum_i (A_i/k_{\text{cat},i})\,v_i \le A_\text{ETC}$ driven by a
per-strain table, where configuration F is one column of that table rather than a second module.
P3 gated it on measured *E. coli* respiration [M1].

K4 carried it to the four *Candida* strains, which is what §6a of the discussion notes had wanted
for months. **It cannot carry the interspecies comparison**, for two independent reasons, and
neither is the one anticipated [M3]. Structurally, in three of the four models the chain carries
no load, so an area budget on ETC flux has nothing to bind on — the same proton-circuit defect as
§[-@sec-shortcuts], seen from a different direction. Parametrically, no measured fungal ETC
footprint or mitochondrial inner-membrane area exists. Re-tested with both escape routes closed,
the required area factor is **122-fold** and still points the wrong way [M4].

Also worth recording: **alternative oxidase is in all four proteomes and in none of the four
models** [M2] — the one genuinely fungal branch of the ETC, and the mechanism Xiao et al. propose,
has no reaction to attach a footprint to.

# Sampling, and a quantity that is not well defined {#sec-sampling}

**No chain in this family is converged, and that applies evenly.** The nine refits run
τ 146–245 against 1500–2000 steps — chain/τ 6–12 against the ≥40 criterion [P1]. Measured with the
same estimator, **all six of Parsa's committed chains** give chain/τ 8.2–9.4, n_eff 148–170 [P2].
Both families have run about nine autocorrelation times. Reaching the criterion is ~8000 steps,
≈40 h for all nine [P3]. This is a sampling-budget property, not a failure of model or diligence,
and the arithmetic is given so the decision to spend it is a considered one.

**And a sharper problem underneath it, found by P6's pre-flight** [EF1] *(on branch
`p6/convergence`; PROVISIONAL-ON-P6 as to location, not as to measurement)*. For configurations E
and F the log-likelihood **varies by 0.13–7.49 at a fixed parameter vector**, against a posterior
width of about 7. The growth term is stable; the **O₂ uptake is not** — it differs by up to
9.4 mmol gDW⁻¹ h⁻¹ on a mean of 19.8 between repeats at the same vector. The cause is identified:
the model's O₂ uptake at optimal growth is **not unique**, and which vertex the solver returns
depends on the basis left by the previous solve. Configurations E and F restructure the problem on
every call (remove and re-add the area constraint); configuration D does not, and its jitter is
≤0.0004.

So the "respiration R²" those chains report was scored on a quantity the model does not determine.
**This does not touch the P3 gate as a port check** — it evaluates one point once after a fresh
build on both sides — and it does not touch configuration D. It does mean that any respiration
conclusion from configuration E or F needs the degeneracy resolved first, by fixing the flux
distribution (a secondary objective, or parsimonious FBA) rather than by longer chains.

# Defects this project introduced {#sec-own}

Seven, listed because the document's credibility depends on their being here rather than in a
footnote. Two changed a conclusion.

| | what | how it surfaced |
|---|---|---|
| O1 | a default flip broke `etcgem tpc` outright for every gecko-provider strain with sectors | the next prompt's own merge verification, before it was pushed |
| O2 | `cli.main` returned the output path into `sys.exit()`, so every successful run exited 1 | it made a verification pass silently vacuous — `cmd && check` skipped the run and compared a file with itself |
| O3 | **the wrong ETC table was wired as configuration F** | the P3 gate; his fits use configuration E's table plus one column |
| O4 | a gate run left an overlay's carbon cap on, so E and F silently carried a cap they were never fitted with | it made NLDM look irreproducible (respiration R² −2.5); caught before any conclusion was drawn |
| O5 | the warm start failed silently in all nine refits | chains started at the emergent point, lengthening burn-in; repaired |
| O6 | **K5's activation-energy sign result did not stand** | K6 checked the comparator: two measured activation energies are not the same quantity |
| O7 | a prompt's own headline table did not survive its test | K9 corrected it: the interspecies requirement is arithmetic |

O3 and O6 changed conclusions. O2 is the instructive one: it did not corrupt a number, it
disabled a *check*, and the check then reported success. The standing responses adopted are
(i) read settings back from the resolved config rather than assuming them, (ii) never verify with
`cmd && check`, and (iii) a generated provenance stamp on every report [R2], because the audit
that started this found **8 of 11** input directories no longer reproducing [R1].

# What is missing {#sec-gaps}

Three kinds, because they need different responses.

## Measurement gaps — no amount of modelling closes these

| what is missing | what it would license | cost |
|---|---|---|
| **a measured meltome for any *Candida*** | replaces the load-bearing predictor with data; would settle §[-@sec-figure] directly | a thermal proteome profiling experiment |
| **per-protein *S. cerevisiae*/*S. uvarum* Tm** | A1's strongest test — the correlation of measured against predicted *differences* | an email to the authors |
| **mitochondrial inner-membrane area per gDW, per species, at 30 and 40 °C** | the measurement an ETC-area budget actually consumes; without it the mechanism is parameterised from *E. coli* | electron microscopy / organelle fractionation |
| **measured fungal ETC footprints and turnovers** | the same, for the table's rows | literature or structure-based estimation |
| **organelle-resolved *Candida* lipidomics** | whole-cell data are rich; fractionated data do not exist | fractionation + lipidomics |
| **the *E. coli* proteome above 37 °C** | removes the bit-identical 37–44 °C shoulder [T6] | extend an existing series |
| **per-cell carbon conversion for the respirometry** | the inoculum back-projection is off in every row, and `cell_volume_um3`/`cell_carbon_fg` are typed constants that disagree with the pipeline's own log by ~6× | a cell-count and dry-weight calibration |

## Model gaps — mechanisms the framework cannot express

* **The membrane as a physical structure.** The area budget is a bound on ETC flux, not a
  representation of a membrane. It cannot express lipid composition, curvature, or the trade-off
  between respiratory and transport machinery for the same surface.
* **Whatever kills cells below the unfolding ceiling.** The model's $CT_\text{max}$ is set by
  enzyme denaturation, and it over-predicts by 9–14 °C. Applying the measured predictor bias
  closes a third to a half [F8]; the residual differs by species [F9] and no uniform correction
  can produce that. Something the model does not contain sets the real limit.
* **Alternative oxidase** [M2], and more generally fungal-specific ETC branches: absent from the
  reconstructions, so absent from every conclusion.
* **The interspecies term is arithmetic** [F6]. The framework as it stands cannot make a
  *difference between species* a model prediction rather than a restatement of the observed
  difference. That is the deepest gap in §[-@sec-figure], and it is structural.

## Housekeeping — known, bounded, and costed

* **Under-converged chains** [P1, P2, P3] — ~40 h for all nine; and for configurations E and F,
  longer chains are the *wrong* fix until the flux degeneracy is resolved [EF1].
* **The unexplained 10 °C** — *Synechocystis*' committed ceiling is not reproducible from a
  strain build (OPEN_ITEMS 3.19); recorded with strain and evidence, not investigated.
* **Stale artefacts** — 8 of 11 directories behind the E. coli report [R1]; the standing fix is
  the provenance stamp, not recomputation, and regeneration is deferred to paper time.
* **`resolved_config.yaml` records an absolute `model_path`**, so "byte-identical on re-run" is
  only checkable from the same directory (OPEN_ITEMS 3.15).

# The publication assessment {#sec-pub}

> **FOR PI JUDGEMENT.** This section lays out the evidence for and against each candidate. It
> reaches no verdict and makes no recommendation on which to pursue. That is deliberate.

## (a) The *Candida* thermal-limit paper

**The claim it would make.** That the growth-limit difference between *C. auris* and its
relatives cannot be explained by the thermostability difference their proteomes carry — the model
requires far more separation than is available.

**Evidence in hand.** The requirement is now stable across model states and repairs: 13.57 °C
[F3], convention-independent [F4], and reproduced by an independent implementation [G1]. The
predictor validation is quantitative and unusually direct [A1–A3, A5, A6]. The corrected fold gap
is 5.4× [2.5, 10.3] [A7] — still a failure of the explanation, on corrected arithmetic.

**What is missing.** A measured *Candida* meltome. Everything on the "available" side is
predicted by a tool shown not to resolve within-proteome variation [A2].

**The strongest referee objection.** *The interspecies requirement is a restatement of the
observed difference, not a model prediction* [F6] — the model's own ceiling spread varies 4.5×
across states while the requirement moves ±3 %. A referee who sees this will ask what the model
contributed. **The defensible form of the claim is per-species**: "this model, with these
predicted stabilities, puts *C. auris*'s thermal ceiling 9.8 °C too high, and the predictor bias
A1 measured accounts for a third to a half of that" [F8]. That is a real model statement and it
survives. The four-species *comparison* is the part that does not.

**A second objection to expect.** The model's growth envelope is too steep by 1.24–2.29× [T7] and
the ΔCp prior accounts for ~88 % of it [T8] — a referee will ask why a parameter known to be
wrong was not corrected before the requirement was computed. The answer available is that the
requirement is insensitive to it (the required-offset spread moves ±3 % across ΔCp −3.0 to −6.0
[F6]), which is a good answer but requires the interspecies framing to be dropped first.

## (b) The *E. coli* gas-flux and overflow work

**The claim it would make.** That gas exchange and overflow can be made determinate and
mechanistic in an enzyme-constrained model, and that a membrane-area budget on the electron
transport chain reproduces measured per-cell respiration.

**Evidence in hand.** Six configurations ported and reproduced [G2, G4]; two independent
mechanisms (carbon cap, membrane area) implemented generically and gated; the O₂-sink correction
[S1]; a real measured dataset in two media, ingested with provenance; and configuration D's
growth fits on M9 among the best in the exercise [C8].

**What is missing, and it is load-bearing.** No chain is converged [P1, P2] — and for
configurations E and F the respiration likelihood is not a function of the parameters [EF1], so
the respiration R² those configurations report is scored on a degenerate quantity. **The
membrane-area result is the headline of this work and it is the one directly affected.**

**The strongest referee objection.** *Your respiration fit is not identifiable.* The answer is
not a longer chain; it is to make the flux distribution unique (a secondary objective or
parsimonious FBA) and refit. That is a bounded piece of work and it is the single highest-value
next step for this line.

**A second objection.** The medium ceiling K is not identified — posterior/prior width 0.57–0.64
[C6] — so the defined medium's carbon ceiling is a prior choice, not a fitted quantity. And
$c_\text{max}$ is medium-dependent in a way that was learned the hard way [C3, C4, C5].

## (c) The cross-organism activation-energy comparison

*Read before assessing: `reports/activation_energy/report.qmd`, which predates this week's work.*

**The claim it makes.** That the ordering methanogenesis > respiration > photosynthesis in
thermal sensitivity arises from three distinct cellular routes — where growth control sits on the
enzyme $E_a$ distribution, and how much the allocation law buffers it — rather than one mechanism
scaled.

**Evidence in hand.** Three organisms, each calibrated to its own measured curve, each
reproducing its observed $E_a$ and the full ordering; a control-weighted decomposition; each
organism's allocation term grounded in its own measured strategy.

**Does this week's work bear on it? Yes, in two specific ways, and one is favourable.**

*Favourable:* the paper quantifies $E_a$ with the **window-independent Sharpe–Schoolfield $E$**.
K6 established independently that this is the valid comparator and that the alternative (an OLS
Arrhenius slope through a curve that turns over) is not — the two differ fourfold on growth and
not at all on respiration [D1]. The paper already uses the convention that survived a test it did
not know it was taking.

*Unfavourable, and it needs an answer:* $E_a$ is a **rising-limb** quantity, and the rising limb
moves with the binding constraint. A carbon cap moved NLDM's $E_a$ from 0.949 to 1.230 eV — +30 %
— between $c_\text{max}$ 80 and 60 [T3]. The paper's three $E_a$ values are each computed at one
operating point per organism. **A referee could ask whether the ordering is a property of the
organisms or of three particular constraint regimes.** The defence is available and should be
made explicitly: each organism is calibrated to its own measured curve, so its operating point is
pinned by data rather than chosen; and the decomposition attributes the ordering to *where control
sits*, which is a structural property. But the question is now on the record and the paper does
not currently address it.

*A third, smaller point:* the *E. coli* strain in that paper is the same one whose report renders
from 8 of 11 directories that no longer reproduce [R1]. Nothing found contradicts a scientific
claim — $T_\text{opt}$, $CT_\text{max}$ and curve shape are stable across every test — but if a
specific number is quoted it should be regenerated first.

## (d) A methods paper on what enzyme-constrained thermal models can and cannot do

**The claim it would make.** That this model class has characteristic, findable failure modes,
and that the checks currently applied to it do not find them.

**The material.** Four uncosted-shortcut instances across three organisms, one in a published
reconstruction [S1–S5]; an audit blind spot that let a free proton circuit pass a clean audit
[S6]; a predictor validated and found to work between organisms and not within a proteome
[A1–A3]; the $T_\text{opt}$/$CT_\text{max}$ asymmetry with its mechanical explanation [T1–T5]; a
likelihood that is not a function of its parameters [EF1]; and a whole family of published and
unpublished chains at ~9 autocorrelation times [P1, P2].

**Being sceptical of this case, as instructed.** There are two ways to read that list.

*As one argument:* every item is an instance of the same thing — **a model-level claim that no
routine check tests**. "Flux costs protein" is falsified by an uncosted route and growth looks
fine. "The optimum is set by stability" is falsified by a change of binding constraint and the
descriptor still has a value. "The fit is good" is falsified by a degenerate objective and R²
still computes. Each failure is silent, each is found only by a check designed for it, and the
paper would be the set of checks. That is a coherent argument with a clear deliverable, and the
class-E audit is proof the checks can be written.

*As a list:* the items are also just things that went wrong in one week on two codebases. The
predictor validation is about a tool, not a model class. The convergence finding is about a
sampling budget and is not specific to thermal models. The $T_\text{opt}$ result is arguably a
restatement of how LP optima work. A referee could reasonably say that three of the five are
generic computational-practice observations that happen to have been made here.

**The strongest referee objection**, if it were written as one argument: *what is the general
claim, and is it tested?* The honest answer is that the general claim would be "these failure
modes are common and current practice does not detect them", and this work supports the second
half far better than the first — it has one deep instance of each, not a survey. **A survey is
what would make it a paper**: run the class-E audit and the shortcut audit across a set of
published GEMs and report the incidence. That is a bounded, well-defined piece of work, and it
would convert a set of anecdotes into a result.

**What is genuinely novel here, and what is not.** Novel: the coupling-ion audit class and its
finding in a published reconstruction; the within-proteome predictor failure measured against a
meltome; the demonstration that a widely-used likelihood is degenerate. Not novel: that GEMs
contain artefacts, that MCMC needs to converge, that LP optima are non-unique. The paper's value
would rest on the first three and on the survey it does not yet have.

# How to update this document {#sec-update}

Re-rendering after P6 lands is the intended workflow.

**Three claims are PROVISIONAL-ON-P6** and have defined slots:

| row | claim | where it lives | what replaces it |
|---|---|---|---|
| [EF1] | the E/F respiration likelihood is not a function of its parameters | §[-@sec-sampling], ¶2 | P6's finished report; if the degeneracy is resolved, the sentence changes from "is not" to "was not, and the fix is X" |
| [C6] | the medium clearance K is not identified | §[-@sec-pub](b) | P6's converged configuration-D posteriors; the width ratio is re-read from `compare_posteriors.csv` |
| [C8] | M9 growth R² 0.959 / 0.987 / 0.982 | §[-@sec-pub](b) | P6's converged configuration-D M9 fit; E and F remain blocked by [EF1] |

**To update:**

1. `python reports/synthesis/build_evidence.py` — re-reads every source file's commit; a row
   whose source has moved gets the new commit automatically.
2. `python reports/synthesis/fig_requirement_arithmetic.py` — only if a *Candida* requirement
   changes; it reads `reports/K7_envelope/task1_conventions.csv`.
3. `quarto render reports/synthesis/synthesis.qmd`.
4. `python scripts/stamp_reports.py`.

**What must not be done silently.** If a number here disagrees with a number in a report, the
disagreement is a finding — `evidence.csv` has a `kind=disagreement` row format for exactly that,
and there are five already. Record it; do not reconcile it by choosing one.
